headings.title: Direct claim, replay and receipt sequence

html:
Execution and receipts

ExecutionEngine.execute_invocation validates the registered argument schema, resolves exact bindings, checks deterministic safety and ExecutionAuthorization, and invokes the tool's executor. Shell commands and Python actions use the Gateway; Python data transforms use a local worker. The database adapter preserves the existing PostgreSQL backend; other adapters use their domain services.

The native caller records a dispatch claim in the run's state authority before execution. The run store retains the receipt and exact artifact with operation ID, canonical capability ID, status, execution/completion flags, actual data, authorization metadata and binding provenance. On the default RAM runtime, those state publications become crash-recoverable through asynchronous saved generations; an accepted claim is not a synchronous disk write. See state and recovery for the durability boundary. Bounded model/UI observations never replace the exact stored result. A successful launch is not a completed job.

The engine's result store is a separate transient cache by default. It holds adapter payload references and previews in process memory and performs no run-scope authorization. Native callers assemble authoritative receipts through the run repository; exact input bindings read that scoped authority, not an arbitrary cached reference. The engine therefore separates validation, adapter dispatch and result retention from the native caller's claim/receipt lifecycle.

A provider adapter must raise UnknownEffectError if a mutating operation may have happened but its outcome cannot be established. The runtime records the uncertainty and requires reconciliation. A crash after a claim has the same protection; it does not imply exactly-once external execution.

Effects, authorization and scope remain deterministic. A tool's description or learned preference cannot override them. Provider-specific validation belongs in its adapter/service, and conservative read/write policy in the execution layer.

For filesystem tools, Native Files and mutation receipts explains selected-Gateway ownership, path namespaces, revision preconditions, staged replacement, partial writes and recovery after a lost receipt.

Decision routing before effects

turn_dispatch.py receives the complete decision from model acquisition. It captures an opening plan when provided, then applies Memory-inspection, Plan-finalization and resource-admission gates before choosing the invocation owner. These gates may return correction feedback or a wait without reaching a business claim.

flowchart TD D[Complete model decision] --> G[Run-level decision gates] G --> H{Mixed top-level human interaction?} H -->|Yes| Reject[Reject every sibling before effects] H -->|No| R[Resource-admission interception] R --> Kind{Invocation shape} Kind -->|Ordinary capability, target, batch or graph| A[Shared Activity dispatcher] Kind -->|Native control or supported single interactive Shell| Single[Direct-call preparation] A --> AcceptA[Accept batch under decision fence] Single --> AcceptD[Accept protocol under decision fence] AcceptA --> Admit[Preflight, dependencies and resource admission] Admit --> Claim[Claim exact call and operation identity] AcceptD --> Claim Claim --> Existing{Existing receipt?} Existing -->|Yes| Reuse[Return retained evidence or unknown-outcome rejection] Existing -->|No| Execute[Guarded control or capability execution] Execute --> Receipt[Publish result and lifecycle evidence] Receipt --> History[Incorporate bounded observation] Reuse --> History

The normal capability path uses Activities even for a single ordinary call. An explicitly selected target also uses that owner. A single interactive or terminal Shell call can retain its direct owner; this does not waive its existing authorization. A top-level ask_user or request_resource_access call mixed with sibling calls is rejected before any batch or receipt claim. An explicitly declared dependency graph has its own supported human-wait semantics, described in jobs and waits.

Direct claim, replay and receipt sequence

sequenceDiagram participant L as Owned AgentLoop participant D as Direct dispatcher participant S as Native run store participant X as Guarded operation or control L->>D: Complete single-call decision D->>D: Validate metadata and canonicalize dispatch copy D->>S: Accept protocol under current decision fence alt Acceptance lost to Pause or steering D->>D: Remove tentative message and pending call D-->>L: Stop or re-arbitrate without an effect else Decision accepted D->>S: Claim call ID and operation under run lease alt Same call ID has different accepted arguments S-->>D: ReusedCallMismatch D-->>L: Protocol feedback, original receipt preserved else Existing receipt or unresolved claim S-->>D: Retained result or outcome_unknown D->>D: Mark reuse nonfresh or reject unsafe replay D-->>L: Existing evidence, no new invocation else New claim S-->>D: Claim accepted D->>X: Validate and dispatch through existing guards X-->>D: Actual result, wait or explicit rejection D->>S: Record receipt for this call identity D->>D: Recheck cancellation before progression D-->>L: Incorporate result or stop progression end end Note over S: Claim acceptance does not guarantee exactly-once external execution

Protocol fields such as output intent and direct completion metadata are extracted before business-argument validation. Deterministic argument/Python normalization changes the dispatch copy and records corrections; it preserves the provider's original business-call text in the model journal. Invalid protocol metadata cannot become an executable business receipt.

Receipt reuse is delivery of existing evidence. It is not a fresh observation and cannot reset the bounded correction path. A changed call identity cannot overwrite the original receipt. Stop can prevent the next model decision even when a tool has already returned a real result; cancellation does not erase that effect.

Shared Activity execution sequence

activities.py owns batch construction, accepted Activity identities, worker launch and ordered joining. Dependency graphs and resource admission keep their own eligibility rules. The sequence below follows one eligible Activity after batch acceptance.

sequenceDiagram participant D as Activity dispatcher participant S as Native state participant A as Dependency and resource admission participant W as Activity worker participant X as execute_claimed D->>S: Accept batch, child identities and output intent D->>D: Preflight batch and apply conflict policy alt Strict conflict or invalid group D->>S: Retain blocked batch without execution else Eligible work D->>A: Submit ready Activity A->>A: Wait for dependencies, target and resource capacity A->>W: Admit with captured target context W->>W: Recheck Stop, current wait and admission facts W->>S: Save Activity intent before dispatch W->>S: Claim exact child call under run lease W->>X: Execute new claim or reuse existing receipt X-->>W: Result and physical lifecycle facts W->>S: Save Activity result, wait or background-job state W->>A: Request resource settlement using retained evidence D->>S: Join parent observations in accepted call order end Note over W: Physical I/O can release the in-process Activity lock Note over A: A worker return alone does not prove an external job ended

Independent graph branches can proceed during a human wait when their dependencies and authority permit it; dependent work waits for the answer. For ordinary waves, the parallel policy bounds worker concurrency. A queued/background job or local approval wait remains nonterminal Activity state even after its initial adapter call returns. Joining publishes children in accepted order and can retain a batch across deferred waits. Parent aggregation does not turn a launch acknowledgement into physical completion.

Adapter execution and result retention

sequenceDiagram participant N as Native operation owner participant E as ExecutionEngine participant A as Live authorities participant T as Registered adapter participant R as Result store participant S as Native run store N->>E: Concrete operation identity and scoped inputs E->>E: Validate schema and exact input bindings E->>A: Recheck target, resource, permission and unsafe policy alt Denied, unavailable or approval required A-->>E: Typed preflight result E->>R: Retain result with no-start lifecycle E-->>N: Rejection or approval requirement else Invocation authorized A-->>E: Accepted authority for this invocation E->>E: Consume applicable exact grants and check cancellation E->>T: Invoke deterministic executor T-->>E: Result or typed failure E->>E: Bind lifecycle, diagnostics and artifact metadata E->>R: Retain payload and bounded preview E-->>N: ExecutionResult end N->>S: Publish scoped evidence and call receipt through native owners Note over R: Default result store is transient and has no run authorization Note over S: Native publication and disk checkpoint are distinct

Exact permission/unsafe grants are rechecked and consumed under the authority lock where applicable; adapter work runs after that lock is released. Adapters own provider-specific semantics and successful output validation. The descriptive result_schema is not a generic engine check that can undo an external effect.

Before-dispatch failures can carry explicit executed = false lifecycle proof. An exception after dispatch cannot acquire that proof merely because the worker failed. Publication contention propagates rather than being recast as a failed remote admission. The native owner converts real adapter data into scoped evidence; the default engine cache alone cannot authorize an exact binding or prove a run's operation completed.

Recovering an interrupted Activity

flowchart TD Saved[Saved Activity without a joined result] --> Job{Matching owned job exists?} Job -->|Yes| Observe[Observe existing job and reconcile its receipt] Job -->|No| Intent{Pending and no invocation record?} Intent -->|Yes| Pending[Preserve never-started work for normal eligibility] Intent -->|No| Exact{Retained result or exact evidence?} Exact -->|Yes| Restore[Restore evidence and result projection] Exact -->|No| Domain[Try supported domain reconciliation] Domain --> Found{Authoritative result found?} Found -->|Yes| Restore Found -->|No| Claimed{Invocation claimed or Activity was running?} Claimed -->|Yes| Unknown[Retain outcome_unknown and replay fence] Claimed -->|No| Cancelled[Retain no-execution cancellation result] Observe --> Join[Join known results or retain the wait] Restore --> Join Unknown --> Join Cancelled --> Join Pending --> Admission[Re-enter ordinary admission when eligible]

This is reconciliation of saved identities, not re-execution of an interrupted effect. For example, a committed schedule can be recovered from its existing domain evidence without creating another event. Missing evidence after a claim keeps the outcome unknown, including confirmed substeps of a multi-step provider operation. A pending Activity with no invocation evidence may still be eligible to start; cancellation, strict conflicts and graph state can prevent it. The state guide defines what survives a process loss, and Gateway recovery owns target-side physical evidence.

Command preparation and outcome

Shell request preparation resolves the target working directory, prepares artifact storage, exports bound inputs and selects stdin, privilege and terminal handling. The launch helpers then choose managed-job admission, a detached terminal or a collected command stream. An observability event announcing a start precedes admission; it does not establish that a process ran.

flowchart TD Request[Validated invocation and resolved inputs] --> Prepare[Prepare target context and artifacts] Prepare --> Mode{Execution mode} Mode --> Job[Gateway job admission receipt] Mode --> Detached[Terminal-owned running result] Mode --> Stream[Raw or interactive command stream] Stream --> Collect[Bounded output and progress] Collect --> Receipt{Valid completion receipt?} Receipt -->|Yes| Result[Verified process outcome] Receipt -->|No| Unknown[Outcome cannot be established]

Stream collection bounds captured stdout, stderr and error text to 1 MiB of characters and retains the process, resource and target facts from completion. Sending cancellation is best effort; receipt validation establishes the subsequent process state. A disconnected or malformed stream cannot be treated as successful completion. Detached execution returns a running result without an exit code, while successful job admission may still represent queued or running work.

For eligible read-only commands, a noninteractive probe is an actual execution attempt. If its result indicates terminal input is required, the runtime may execute the command again in the available terminal. Without that terminal it returns resumable guidance, with separate configuration facts for scheduled or durable tasks. Managed jobs bypass this probe path.

Gateway command streams

The ordinary Gateway executor validates cwd, prepares managed temporary-directory mapping and creates a separately owned shell process. Windows uses cmd or the PowerShell exit-code wrapper; POSIX uses the configured shell's login-command mode. Request environment overlays the Gateway process environment; local privilege has a stricter boundary described below.

Two pipe-reader threads feed one 64-entry queue. Each read is bounded to 16,384 characters, with backpressure while the consumer is slow. A short prompt without a newline can still wait for more input or EOF. The buffered API retains at most 1 MiB of UTF-8 stdout/stderr bytes combined; this differs from the Controller's character-count stream preview described above.

Cancellation is registered before or after process creation under one shared lock. POSIX termination targets the owned process group and escalates to KILL even if its shell leader already exited; Windows uses its process-tree implementation. A cancellation acknowledgement reports a request/known handle, not successful completion. Closing the stream cleans up its owned process and registry entry. The ordinary pipe path can still wait on descriptors retained by descendants after the leader exits; it does not promise a bounded post-exit drain.

Gateway job lifecycle explains admission, worker ownership, completion receipts and uncertain effects. Terminal execution covers the distinct persistent terminal and managed TTY implementations.

Python actions and local transforms

Python action preparation packages main(inputs) and its bound values into a target-shell command. The Gateway owns its process, working directory, streaming and cancellation. Source validation parses code without executing it; syntax diagnostics expose numeric positions and fixed error text instead of candidate source lines.

execute_transform instead sends transform(inputs) to a separate local worker. Sandbox policy restricts builtins, imports and attribute access; budget policy independently controls resource enforcement. With budgets enforced, the parent limits the request to 4 MiB and clamps elapsed time to 0.1–30 seconds. The worker limits address space to 256 MiB, CPU time to five seconds and encoded output to 1 MiB. The parent terminates and reaps the child on success, failure, timeout or cancellation. The worker imports Unix resource facilities: the Windows command wrapper for Python actions does not establish Windows support for local transforms.

Python source correction

The Python canonicalizer runs after generic tool-argument normalization and before claims, effects, authorization or execution. The default-ON Automatic Python correction preference is captured per accepted task and survives resume and restart. Already-valid source and setting-OFF calls remain byte-for-byte unchanged. Two correction paths have different contracts:

  • Conservative wrapping and relocation handles simple scripts and a bounded class of plain synchronous helpers, moves eligible import/helper preludes into a sole entrypoint, and removes an exact redundant trailing call or guard. It analyzes lexical bindings, helper escape and definite outer reads. Transforms require these rules; existing-entrypoint repairs also remain conservative.
  • Generic missing-main run wrapping applies only to python.run / python__run when the conservative wrapping proof declines source. It treats the entire original AST body as an intended main(inputs) body, retaining statement order and literal values without proving module/function equivalence. Callbacks, default arguments, annotations, nested definitions and ordinary control flow can qualify. It does not invent a return or call an otherwise unused helper.

The run path rejects conflicting bare main references/bindings before generating a wrapper. A candidate is compiled without executing it and must pass the existing validator. A generic wrapper whose compiled entrypoint is a generator/coroutine is refused because the runner invokes main once; nested generator helpers can still be valid. Module-only syntax that cannot nest is refused. Transform sandbox policy and all later effect/permission checks remain independent of correction.

Refusal returns the exact original source without a successful correction event. The generic rule ID is python.run.wrap_missing_main_generic, with correction kind wrap_missing_entrypoint. Passing correction does not establish runtime success: for example, a forward local read may still raise UnboundLocalError. An execution failure remains its ordinary result rather than an instruction to rerun the code. The source fixtures cover these distinctions; the V2 report retains the earlier conservative proof and its historical measurements.

The raw model journal remains exact. Canonical business source is used for Activity/parallel/dependency children, replay comparison, operation claims, safety, authorization and receipt arguments. python.code_canonicalized records only tool identity and stable correction metadata. Correction adds no model or Gateway call and is not execution evidence. Only actual execution can establish a receipt.

EFFECT_CLASSIFIER_REVISION versions persisted Shell classifications. Literal subshell boundaries terminate redirect operands outside quotes; (git status 2>/dev/null) remains read-only, while real file outputs and dynamic destinations remain conservative. Reclassifying a historical job updates derived effect facts and audit history, never its execution outcome.

Agent scheduling and Gateway admission share execution/resources.py overlap semantics. Gateway derives bounded literal filesystem paths, aliases and hardlink identities on the target; unsupported commands use *. Launch CWD is retained for compatibility, rather than treated as proof that two mutations affect the same or different resources.

Shell effect analysis reuses execution/shell_syntax.py for literal structure and shell_operations.py for executable/argument semantics. execution/remote_shell.py recognizes a bounded SSH invocation, optionally wrapped in sshpass, with one literal remote program argument. effects.py classifies that program through the same canonical classifier, propagating reads, mutations and unknowns through at most four SSH layers. Unsupported options, dynamic arguments and interactive SSH cannot establish a read proof. This execution analysis is separate from verified SSH working-context identity; it does not modify transport, credentials, shared executable discovery or Gateway registration.

Literal authentication and unsafe approval

Shell accepts literal sudo_password and sudo_username arguments. The Gateway reports actual credential_required, credential_rejected, privilege_not_permitted, and execution/uncertainty facts. The Agent can ask one ordinary question after such a result and retry on its next normal decision.

Unsafe confirmation collects approval only. After a proven unexecuted authentication failure, the authority owner can retain a digest-bound grant for the same operation with only its password changed. The original five-minute expiry and policy still apply, with at most three retained retries. Command/code, username, cwd, target, Gateway or authority changes invalidate it. Unknown effects cannot retain it. Successful sequence prefixes are referenced by their receipts and never replayed.

Foreground execution closes its per-command supervision scope upon receiving a completion receipt or losing the stream. completed is a transport event, not a success classification: an unknown outcome remains unknown. Gateway process-tree identity determines physical ownership; supervision and historical effects are separate. See resource wait recovery.

Local privilege transport

Local privilege execution supports POSIX hosts. If a username is supplied, it must identify the Gateway's current OS account; it does not select an arbitrary target account. An already-root Gateway uses the direct execution path. Otherwise, the wrapper invokes sudo with a fresh authentication check, private stdin when a password is supplied, and noninteractive mode when it is absent. Passwords are not placed in shell argv or environment. The target's stdin is closed before execution so it cannot consume the authentication input.

Only the exact PRIVILEGED_RUNTIME_METADATA_KEYS bindings are accepted from the request. Unsupported variables and NUL-containing values are refused before launch; they are not silently discarded or accepted because of an OF_ prefix. The nonroot launcher receives its own fixed locale, then exports approved metadata inside the elevated child. Remote SSH elevation has a separate working-context contract.

A fresh stderr marker distinguishes elevation from authentication diagnostics. Early stdout is held under a bounded allowance until that marker is observed. Private wrappers and markers are filtered even when split across stream chunks; pre-elevation sudo diagnostics and internal exception details are not returned. Literal text deliberately printed by the target remains ordinary output, including text that matches a supplied credential. This transport is not a general-purpose secret redactor.

Buffered and streamed responses share the same classifier and combined 1 MiB UTF-8 output allowance. After elevation, the command owns its actual exit code; a nonzero command result is not reclassified as bad credentials. A missing receipt or unrecognized pre-elevation failure remains unknown_effect. Consumers must use that uncertainty rather than treating an unobserved elevation marker as proof that no side effect occurred.

Observe-only assessment

Optional monitoring separates a disabled check's native assessment from its enforcement. Path assessment retains the configured root while dispatching the same disabled-mode path. Strict schema and transform static assessment retain the relaxed/unsandboxed execution path and execute only once. Permission and unsafe-action assessment add no approval interaction. Duration and generation thresholds are observed at existing callbacks or operation completion; monitoring installs no cancellation deadline and leaves provider termination authoritative.

Gateway policy carries the captured monitoring bit in authenticated internal metadata. Bounded observations return in HTTP headers, internal SSE events or outbound session frame metadata. The controller strips this metadata before producing tool results and records normal Activity; Gateways do not write Agent UI state. These diagnostics make no additional model calls or remote executions.

Controller observation boundary

inspect_execution is a read-only native control over retained SMTO identities. It bypasses target resource admission, effect-conflict preflight and Gateway/Python/Shell dispatch, and creates no execution receipt or scheduler reservation. Its bounded result reports lifecycle, dependencies, capacity dimensions/blockers, liveness, progress and evidence freshness. It cannot establish a new target fact or reconcile an uncertain effect. Capability guidance prefers this control for status questions; no natural-language interceptor or helper model call substitutes for the Agent's normal tool choice.

Proven inspection resource claims reuse Shell structural/effect facts. Audited ps, pgrep, lsof, stat, readlink, realpath and finite head/tail reads use lightweight capacity; proven cat, wc, du, find and checksum scans use disk-read capacity. Unsupported flags, output writes, executable helpers, dynamic wrappers, unknown programs and background launches retain their existing effectful/unknown demands. The default unknown budget remains one. A read effect is not permission to skip global/run/Gateway ceilings or authorization.

Delivery is separate from execution

The global head/tail preview allowance changes the model's view of stored results. Commands, permissions, schedules, input bindings, job supervision and cancellation keep their existing execution paths. A shortened output does not prove a background process finished, and a successful projection does not resolve unknown external effects. Context overflow preserves receipts and never automatically repeats completed work.
